original_value: This paper presents Amateur, an augmented reality based vehicle navigation system using commodity smart phones. Amateur reads the navigation information from a digital map, matches it into live road condition video captured by smart phone, and directly annotates the navigation instructions on the video stream. The Amateur design entails two major challenges, including the lane identification and the intersection inference so as to correctly annotate navigation instructions for lane-changing and intersection-turning. In this paper, we propose a particle filter based design, assisted by inertial motion sensors and lane markers, to tolerate incomplete and even erroneous detection of road conditions. We further leverage traffic lights as land markers to estimate the position of each intersection to accurately annotate the navigation instructions. We develop a prototype system on Android mobile phones and test our system in a total number of more than 300km travel distance on different taxi cabs in a city. The evaluation results suggest that our system can timely provide correct instructions to navigate drivers. Our system can identify lanes in 2s with 92.7% accuracy and detect traffic lights with 95.29% accuracy. Overall, the accuracy of the navigation signs placement is less than 105 pixels on the screen throughout the experiments. The feedback from 50 taxi drivers indicates that Amateur provides an improved experience compared to traditional navigation systems.

result.paraphrase: This paper introduces Amateur, an augmented-reality vehicle navigation system built for commodity smartphones. It pulls navigation data from a digital map, aligns it with live road-condition video captured by a smartphone, and overlays the navigation instructions directly onto the video stream. Amateur faces two main challenges: lane identification and intersection inference, both needed to annotate lane changes and intersection turns correctly. To handle incomplete and even faulty road-condition detection, we propose a particle-filter-based approach aided by inertial motion sensors and lane markers. We also use traffic lights as landmarks to estimate each intersection’s position, enabling more accurate navigation instruction annotation. A prototype was developed on Android phones and evaluated over more than 300 km of travel in different taxi cabs in one city. The results show that the system can provide timely, correct driving instructions. It identifies lanes in 2 seconds with 92.7% accuracy and detects traffic lights with 95.29% accuracy. Across the experiments, navigation sign placement stayed within less than 105 pixels on the screen. Feedback from 50 taxi drivers shows that Amateur offers a better experience than traditional navigation systems.
